elements.quote: Cancer is a complex, multilevel phenomenon [1-5] in which health outcomes depend on highly interrelated elements across stages of etiology, prevention, screening, diagnosis, treatment, survivorship, and end-of-life care [6, 7]. Standard bench and clinical research approaches alone are not well suited to account for this complexity, as most cancer control interventions often focus on explicit, often linear health outcomes of a specific, well-defined population [1, 8, 9]. To overcome persistent barriers to providing high-quality, equitable care, approaches are needed to address this complexity and provide guidance for successful intervention.
elements.reason: The introduction explicitly describes the current state of knowledge (cancer is complex, multilevel) and gaps/uncertainties (standard approaches not well suited; need for approaches that address complexity).

elements.quote: In a 2019 report, the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine argued that systems science methods could help illustrate the multilevel nature of cancer effects and costs to society and help cancer control efforts be more agile and adaptive [7]. The Journal of the National Cancer Institute published several reports calling for the use of complex, multilevel, or systems-focused approaches to advance the landscape of cancer prevention and control [1, 2, 10]. Systems models, particularly well calibrated simulation models, provide a relatively lowcost and low-risk opportunity for comparing potential interventions or treatments in silico before involving busy clinics and patients in trials [1, 7, 11, 12]. ... The extent to which system dynamics modeling has been applied specifically to cancer prevention and control has not been studied.
elements.reason: The authors justify the review by citing authoritative calls for systems approaches, describing advantages of systems models, and stating that the extent of system dynamics use in cancer prevention and control has not been studied — establishing the importance and need for this review.
No explicit discussion or citation of prior similar systematic reviews or explanation of how this review updates or replicates previous reviews is present in the retrieved evidence.

The review is a methods review of system dynamics modeling applications rather than a review of intervention effects; no proposed mechanism of action for an intervention is relevant or provided in the retrieved evidence.
The review does not focus on a specific complex intervention or delivery context and does not present a logic model; requirement therefore does not apply based on the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: Included articles: 1) were published in peer-reviewed journals; 2) were written in English; 3) used system dynamics modeling (i.e., causal-loop diagramming, stock-and-flow diagramming, or computational system dynamics modeling); 4) pertained to cancer prevention or control; and 4) were published within the last 10 years.
elements.reason: The manuscript specifies several study characteristics used for eligibility (publication type, language, use of system dynamics modeling, topical focus, and publication year window). It does not, however, specify other study characteristics requested by the criterion (e.g., eligible study designs beyond system-dynamics types, settings, or any follow-up requirements), so the element is only partially satisfied.

elements.quote: Included articles: 1) were published in peer-reviewed journals; 2) were written in English; ... and 4) were published within the last 10 years.
elements.reason: The review explicitly reports eligibility criteria for report characteristics: publication status (peer-reviewed), language (English), and dissemination year (published within the last 10 years).
No evidence was found distinguishing exclusion due to outcomes not being measured versus exclusion due to outcome results not being reported.

elements.quote: As shown in Fig 1, most studies included a computational system dynamics simulation model (n = 21; 66%), while the remaining studies (n = 11; 34%) used only diagramming approaches (referred to as diagram-only studies in this review). ... The purpose of models developed in the included studies spanned understanding complex dynamics of the problem, identifying or assessing potential interventions, evaluating a past intervention, predicting or estimating outcomes, summarizing the literature, building consensus, preparing for simulation, identifying research gaps, and demonstrating the potential of system dynamics as a method.
elements.reason: The review specifies groupings used in synthesis (e.g., simulation vs diagram-only, and topic/purpose clusters) and provides counts. However, it does not explicitly link these groups to predefined comparisons in the review objectives (no explicit statement linking groups to objective-defined comparisons), so the requirement is only partially met.

elements.quote: This search period was selected to reflect recent developments and current applications of system dynamics modeling related to cancer.
elements.reason: The manuscript provides a rationale for a notable restriction on eligibility (limiting included studies to the last 10 years) explaining it was chosen to reflect recent developments and current applications.

elements.quote: Searches for peer-reviewed publications were conducted between February and April 2022 through the PubMed, Scopus, and APA PsycInfo databases using the search terms 'cancer' AND ("causal loop" OR "system dynamics * " OR "systems thinking" OR "group model * ").
elements.reason: The manuscript reports an overall date range for when searches were conducted (February to April 2022) and lists databases searched, but does not report the specific date on which each individual information source was last searched or consulted.

elements.quote: Searches for peer-reviewed publications were conducted between February and April 2022 through the PubMed, Scopus, and APA PsycInfo databases
elements.reason: The names of the bibliographic databases searched are reported, but the manuscript does not report the search interface/platform used for each database nor the available coverage dates for each database.
No study registers, regulatory databases, or online repositories are reported as having been searched in the provided evidence, so this item does not apply to the reported information sources.

elements.quote: Additional searches were conducted in eight journals ( System Dynamics Review , American Journal of Public Health , the Journal of the Operational Research Society , Systems Research and Behavioral Science , Health Research Policy & Systems , BMCHealth Services Research , Journal of the National Cancer Institute , and Cancer ).
elements.reason: The manuscript names journals searched but does not report any website/search engine names with URLs or provide URLs for the listed journal sources; thus required URL information for online sources is missing.

There is no evidence that organisations or manufacturers were contacted to identify studies; the review used database, journal, citation, and author searches, so contacting organisations/manufacturers does not apply.

The manuscript does not report contacting types of individuals to identify studies (e.g., experts, clinicians) for the literature search; thus this reporting item does not apply based on the provided evidence.

elements.quote: Articles were also identified via a 'snowball' method through citation and author searching.
elements.reason: The authors state that a 'snowball' method using citation and author searching was used, which indicates reference-list checking, but they do not specify the types of reference lists examined (e.g., reference lists of included studies, reviews) in detail.

elements.quote: To our knowledge, this was the first study to systematically review prior applications of system dynamics modeling across the cancer control continuum. In their review of system dynamics models pertaining to public health and medicine, Darabi and Hosseinichimeh [17] identified a handful of studies using system dynamics modeling to replicate clinical trials and simulate different interventions related to cancer, noting that this area is 'generally underexplored' and would likely benefit from further development of models for cancer screening and treatment. Similar to the findings of our paper, this review found that only a fraction of disease-related modeling studies published their model equations and methodology for development. In a scoping review of system dynamics studies related to addiction, Naumann and colleagues [65] found similarly that the method has been underutilized and that participant engagement should be further used in future studies. In their review of system dynamics models used to assess economic efficiency in public health, Jadeja and colleagues [11] also found underutilization of participatory approaches. In a study of system dynamics applications across business, environment, and health care domains, Zanker and colleagues [27] also found weak verification and validation of models published in articles that provided little or no methodological details outlining model development. These omissions threaten the validity of the specific models being described, as well as the perceived credibility and value of modeling as a method. Stange and colleagues' [1] literature review outlined global observations and opportunities for multilevel interventions across the cancer control continuum. As in our review, the authors noted a greater focus on topics around prevention and screening, as opposed to other areas along the continuum, like cancer survivorship.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly compares its findings to multiple prior reviews and studies, noting similarities (e.g., underutilization, lack of methodological detail, focus on prevention/screening) and placing its results in the context of existing evidence.

elements.quote: This study has several limitations. In bounding our review to studies published in the last 10 years, we excluded older studies that could have contributed to this synthesis. We also excluded studies related to topics such as nutrition and physical activity if they did not include cancer in their models or research aims. While we feel this narrowed criteria was helpful in maintaining focus, inclusion of models more tangentially related to cancer might have provided a more comprehensive understanding of the current range of research. Due to our focus on cancer prevention and control, we also excluded studies that were solely related to cancer pathogenesis; if these were included, far more studies would be categorized as relating to etiology in the cancer control continuum. Our understanding of the applications of modeling covered in the included studies was also limited by the descriptions included in the articles themselves, which were shaped by journal audience. Our quality ratings, therefore, reflected both modeling and reporting. Finally, the diversity of model purposes, types, and applications presented a challenge to adapting the quality assessment criteria. While we chose to apply a universal set of criteria to included studies to enable comparison, future research could further specify tailored criteria (e.g., based on model purpose).
elements.reason: The Limitations section explicitly discusses multiple limitations of the evidence included in the review (time window exclusion, topic exclusions, exclusion of pathogenesis studies, limited reporting in source articles, and heterogeneity of models impacting quality assessment).
